#6551. Why Did Early Humans Collect Strange Stones 500,000 Years Ago? Scientists Have a New Theory

Prehistoric discoveries in Israel raise the possibility that keeping meaningful objects helped early humans distinguish personal memories from stories and gradually develop a sense of identity.

A stone picked up during a hike or a seashell brought home from the beach might seem ordinary to everyone else. Yet years later, that small object can bring back memories of where you were, who you were with, and what made the experience special. It’s a familiar human habit, and researchers now believe its origins may reach back nearly half a million years.

A new study from Tel Aviv University suggests that early humans may have collected and kept objects for much the same reason we do today. The researchers propose that these prehistoric keepsakes could have helped shape our ability to remember personal experiences and develop a sense of who we are.

The idea emerged from archaeological discoveries at several prehistoric sites in Israel, where researchers found colorful stones, unusual handaxes, and much older tools that appeared to have been collected despite offering no obvious practical benefit.

At Qesem Cave, for example, small, colorful pebbles had been brought in from different locations. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological patterns. Some were carefully shaped so that these distinctive features remained at the center, where they could be seen and touched.

Other discoveries offer an intriguing connection to the past. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, researchers identified older flint tools that had apparently been collected after their surfaces had changed with age. Although some were resharpened, much of their original surfaces and evidence of earlier workmanship remained intact.

Why would someone keep an old tool when they could make a new one? The researchers suggest that its age and appearance may have been part of its appeal. Just as an old family heirloom can carry meaning beyond its usefulness, these objects might have been valued for the experiences or histories associated with them.

Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology explains the possibility:

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives. In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

There may be a deeper psychological reason why such objects mattered. Our minds do not simply store experiences. They must also distinguish between things we personally experienced, stories we heard from others, and events we imagined.

The researchers propose that seeing or touching a familiar object could have helped early humans make those distinctions. A stone collected from a particular location, for instance, might have brought back a personal memory of being there.

That ability could have mattered well beyond individual recollection. Remembering encounters, alliances, gifts, mutual obligations, and rights connected to particular places helps people maintain relationships and cooperate. A keepsake could also be carried elsewhere and shown to others, potentially making a personal account more convincing and helping establish trust.

The researchers believe this behavior may have become especially useful as early humans faced changes in their environment.

Prof. Ran Barkai offers one possible explanation:

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle. Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

Over many generations, the researchers suggest, keeping meaningful objects may have placed evolutionary pressure on the brain systems involved in identifying where memories come from and how reliable they are.

In this proposed scenario, objects and memory evolved together. As people increasingly used physical reminders of their experiences, the brain mechanisms supporting personal memory may have become more sophisticated.

That process could have contributed to the development of autobiographical memory, our ability to connect individual experiences into a continuing story of our lives. It is an important part of how we understand our identities and our relationships with others.

The researchers emphasize that their interpretation remains a hypothesis. An unusual stone or carefully preserved tool does not necessarily prove that its owner associated it with a personal memory. The archaeological evidence cannot reveal exactly what someone was thinking hundreds of thousands of years ago.

However, the findings suggest that the habit of keeping meaningful objects may date back roughly 500,000 years, long before written records or photographs.

And if the researchers’ interpretation is correct, the simple act of keeping a stone from a memorable place may once have played a role in the evolution of how humans remember their lives.

Reference: “Homo Memorabiliaxis: Souvenirs and the Evolution of Autobiographical Memory and Self” by Ran Barkai, Ella Assaf, Bar Efrati, Tal Simon, Liad Mudrik and Yoav Ram, 19 October 2026, Evolutionary Anthropology: Issues, News, and Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/evan.70051

#6550. The Origins of Wealth Inequality May Go Back 5,000 Years, Ancient Graves Reveal

The roots of inherited privilege may reach back thousands of years, with ancient graves revealing how one European community gradually became more divided by wealth and status.

Among nearly 300 prehistoric graves examined in Bohemia, the richest belonged to a young girl. Buried alongside her was an exceptionally rare copper neck ring, an object that raises an intriguing question about life thousands of years ago. Was she born into a wealthy family, or did her elaborate burial reflect something else about how her community valued status?

For archaeologists, questions like these are difficult to answer because prehistoric societies left behind no census records, tax registers, or written accounts of who held wealth and power.

A new archaeological method is helping researchers piece together that missing history by examining how people buried their dead. Developed by University of Copenhagen archaeologist Mikkel Nørtoft during his PhD research, QuantWealth combines multiple forms of archaeological evidence to reconstruct social status, displays of wealth, and inequality. In a study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology, Nørtoft and his colleague Adam B. Rohrlach applied the method to 296 graves belonging to the Corded Ware culture in present-day Bohemia, dating from approximately 2900 to 2300 BCE.

The researchers examined burial practices and grave goods alongside genetic ancestry, Y-chromosome patterns that trace paternal lineages, and skeletal evidence of age, sex, and pathological conditions. By comparing these different clues, they could investigate how social differences changed across several centuries. The findings suggest that inequality developed gradually rather than emerging as a firmly established social hierarchy when migrants from the eastern European steppe settled in the region.

The Corded Ware culture formed part of a much larger transformation in prehistoric Europe, when populations migrating from the steppe helped spread early Indo-European dialects across the continent. Archaeologists have debated whether these newcomers also introduced strongly patriarchal societies in which wealth and power passed primarily through family lines. The evidence from Bohemia points toward a more complicated history.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy. Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually. Achieving status through life-actions appears to have been more important than through inheritance, at least during the first 400 years”, says Nørtoft, the study’s lead author.

During the earliest period, approximately 2900 to 2700 BCE, burial practices suggest that the newly established communities placed considerable emphasis on shared traditions. Differences in grave wealth were relatively small and largely associated with age. There was little evidence of pronounced gender inequality, and power appeared to be distributed among several paternal lineages with steppe ancestry.

Nørtoft connects this early pattern to the circumstances surrounding the migrants’ arrival in Central Europe.

“Following a few harsh years of ‘dark sun’ clouded by a devastating volcanic eruption 2,900 BCE, the earliest herder communities, settling in Bohemia around 2,900-2,700 BCE, seem to have focused mostly on building social cohesion across this new network of migrants in Central Europe. In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Mikkel Nørtoft explains.

Between approximately 2700 and 2500 BCE, however, burial customs began to change. The appearance of a new paternal lineage coincided with increasingly elaborate funerals, including greater concentrations of prestigious objects and meat offerings. Exchange networks expanded, and differences between male and female burials became more pronounced.

Adult men were particularly likely to receive richly furnished graves, while younger adults became increasingly common among those buried. Despite this growing competition for status, the skeletal evidence did not show a clear corresponding increase in injuries associated with violence.

The final phase, spanning roughly 2500 to 2300 BCE, brought further changes. One paternal lineage had become dominant in the burial record, and a small number of children received unusually wealthy burials. Because children had less opportunity to accumulate status through their own accomplishments, these graves raise the possibility that some families had begun passing social advantages between generations.

“In the final phase, roughly 2,500-2,300 BCE, we see a few rich displays of family wealth through children, and the previously new lineage now dominated the burial record. So maybe the new lineage had gained the most followers and power through the competitive burial parties, and their descendants were now competing among themselves,” Mikkel Nørtoft points out and adds:

“The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality. Ethnographic parallels could also support the idea that parents adorned their children with ornaments to increase their social value in future marriage exchange. Brides often moved into the husband’s household in Corded Ware societies, and bridewealth or dowry is preserved in early Indo-European vocabulary, and historically common in Indo-European societies.”

The extraordinarily rich grave of a young girl at Čachovice offers a particularly striking example of this possible shift. It was the wealthiest burial among all 296 graves examined and contained an extremely rare copper neck ring. Similar neck ornaments, known as torcs, became widespread symbols of upper-class status during the later European Bronze and Iron Ages. The researchers suggest that objects placed in children’s graves may sometimes have reflected family standing or efforts to enhance their social value in future marriage arrangements, although these interpretations remain uncertain.

Taken together, the changing burial patterns suggest that competition for prestige may have gradually created more lasting social divisions within Corded Ware communities. The possibility that wealth and status were becoming hereditary is especially significant because later Bronze Age societies provide evidence of enduring family dynasties. Whether the developments in Bohemia represented early steps toward those systems remains an open question.

Researchers will need additional archaeological and genetic evidence from both the Corded Ware culture and the related Bell Beaker culture, which subsequently replaced it in Central Europe, to determine how closely burial wealth corresponded to inherited family status. The study demonstrates how archaeological evidence, ancient DNA, and linguistic history can be combined to investigate social changes that written records cannot document.

“We now have a correlation between changing Y-haplogroup lineages and unequal burial wealth display in one region, but we need more DNA data to confirm this at the family level, and elsewhere,” explains Nørtoft.

Reference: “Cooperation and Competition: Changes in Wealth, Power, and Patrilines in the Czech Corded Ware Culture” by Mikkel Nørtoft and Adam B. Rohrlach, November 2026, Journal of Neolithic Archaeology. DOI: 10.12766/jna.2026.7

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

She has a DPhil in organic chemistry from the University of Oxford.

#6546. Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

During angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

The research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala said considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

Reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488

#6545. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find New Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions.”

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292

Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

#6542. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6540. Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. In preclinical testing, the experimental nanomaterial produced approximately 80 percent more new bone than a control material after eight weeks.

Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors. Researchers hope the approach could eventually allow children to receive treatment years earlier than is typically possible today.

Cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy. Correcting the resulting jawbone defects is among the most challenging aspects of treatment, with potential consequences for eating, breathing, speech, and social development.

“One of the biggest challenges for children born with cleft lip and palate is repairing the bone defect in the jaw,” said lead researcher Associate Professor Chun Xu, a Sydney Horizon Fellow in the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Medicine and Health.

“While some children with minor defects are treated as infants, many patients need to wait until they are around 10 to 12 years old before surgeons can take bone from another part of the body and graft it into the defect.

“That means many kids live with difficulties for years. It can affect their breathing, eating and speech. Most heartbreaking of all, it can have a huge impact on their confidence and social development.”

More than four million bone repair procedures are performed worldwide annually. Many current treatments rely on bone harvested from the patient or animal-derived materials that primarily provide structural support. The new approach instead aims to stimulate the formation of living bone using a biodegradable calcium-aluminosilicate nanomaterial.

The material activates a naturally occurring growth factor called latent Transforming Growth Factor β1 (TGF-β1). This protein normally exists in an inactive form until biological signals trigger its activity. Once activated, it helps recruit stem cells to the damaged area and encourages their development into bone-producing cells. As new tissue forms, the biodegradable material is gradually replaced by the patient’s own bone.

“The material activates dormant repair signals in the body, triggering a cascade of healing processes that attract bone-forming stem cells and stimulate new bone growth,” Xu explained.

“Our body already contains many of the signals needed for tissue repair,” Associate Professor Xu said.

“We’ve developed a material that can help activate those signals at the right place and time. Instead of supplying external growth factors, we’re encouraging the body to use its own healing potential.”

The study, published in ACS Nano, found that the material activated the body’s latent bone repair growth factor at approximately 10 times the level achieved using conventional methods. It also promoted blood clotting within about 30 seconds, which could help stabilize an injury during the earliest stages of healing.

According to the researchers, this is the first demonstration of a single nanomaterial platform capable of combining rapid blood clotting, activation of naturally occurring growth factors, recruitment of bone-forming stem cells, and enhanced bone regeneration. The findings come from a preclinical bone model, however, and further testing is necessary to determine whether the material can be used safely and effectively in humans.

Xu and his colleagues envision a future in which bone defects can be repaired earlier in childhood, potentially reducing the need to remove healthy bone from elsewhere in the body.

“Our long-term goal is to develop materials that help the body regenerate bone naturally and reduce the need for these invasive and painful procedures. We hope this could allow treatment much earlier than is possible today.”

The researchers are also investigating whether the nanomaterial could be incorporated into personalized 3D-printed scaffolds designed to fit an individual’s bone defect. Beyond cleft lip and palate, potential applications include repairing bone damaged by traumatic injuries, tooth loss, and other conditions involving difficult-to-heal defects.

“Every patient is different, and every bone defect is different,” Xu said.

“In the future, we hope to combine these materials with advanced 3D-printing technologies so treatments can be tailored to the specific needs of each patient.”

The technology remains at the preclinical stage, with additional research required before human trials can begin.

Reference: “Multifunctional Mesoporous Calcium-Aluminosilicate Nanoparticles Enable Heterogeneous Activation of Endogenous Transforming Growth Factor β1 and Rapid Hemostasis for Bone Repair” by Chun Xu, Qingxuan Chen, Hang Chen, Aoni Xu, Juan Wen, Yiwei Li, Huan Dai, Siyuan Liu, Dan Cheng, Yaping Song, Bing Sun, Jie Tang, Jie Fan, Chang Lei and Chengzhong Yu, 15 September 2026, ACS Nano. DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c05126

The authors acknowledge the funding support from Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council and the University of Sydney. A provisional patent application related to the findings reported in this manuscript has been filed by the University of Sydney and the University of Queensland. The application covers calcium-aluminosilicate mesoporous nanoparticles and their use for bone repair, as described in the paper (Provisional Patent Application No. 2026903515).

A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a series of clouds sculpted by von Kármán vortices from a volcano on South Korea's Jeju Island. A giant multicolor plume, ejected by China's Yangtze River, is also visible in the image.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

A recent satellite photo captured a stunning scene of sediment swirling across the West Florida Shelf after an extreme cold snap that covered large parts of the eastern U.S. in snow.

#6538. Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.

Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud. This vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies is thought to contain trillions of objects and extend as far as 1.6 light-years from the Sun.

Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system. In addition to gravitational disturbances caused by passing stars, he suggests that a low-mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) could periodically redirect comets toward the Sun. Under this hypothesis, Nemesis and the Sun orbit a shared center of gravity.

According to Muller, Nemesis follows a slightly elongated orbit that periodically brings it into regions of the Oort Cloud, where its gravity could disrupt the paths of billions of comets.

Muller explained in a phone interview that these encounters could trigger comet showers lasting roughly a million years. The greatest number of comets would be redirected into the inner solar system when Nemesis passes through the cloud’s densest regions.

The proposed Nemesis star is not related to the hypothetical Planet X. It also differs from unrelated stars that occasionally pass near the solar system and gravitationally disturb the Oort Cloud, potentially sending numerous comets inward.

Unlike these unpredictable stellar encounters, the Nemesis hypothesis proposes a recurring cycle. Muller believes this mechanism could explain a pattern of impacts on Earth spanning approximately 250 million years.

Muller points to a 1982 study published in the journal Science by paleontologists David Raup and Jack Sepkoski. The researchers compiled an extensive record of marine extinctions that, according to Muller, revealed a striking pattern of extinction events occurring roughly every 26 million years.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. “Well, maybe there’s a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth,” he says.

It’s an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn’t sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, says Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of France’s Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email.

Planetesimals that originated in our Sun’s planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun’s birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he says.

Many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because it’s moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesn’t show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be big enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means it’s probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, says Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

Yet the evidence that it’s an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that’s what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, “You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?”

He responded, “Sure, we couldn’t tell the difference.”

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long-period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, says Muller.

The bad news is that if it’s out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie coplanar with most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, says Muller.

References: “Dynamical Population of Comet Reservoirs” by Nathan A. Kaib and Kathryn Volk, May 30, 2022, arXiv. DOI: 2206.00010

“Measurement of the lunar impact record for the past 3.5 b.y. and implications for the Nemesis theory” by Richard A. Muller, 01 January 2002, Geological Society of America DOI: 10.1130/0-8137-2356-6.659

“Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record” by David M. Raup and J. John Sepkoski, Jr., 19 March 1982, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.215.4539.1501

#6536. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6535. NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

Didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

These conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

During this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

That day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised important questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

The spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an important role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."
