#6499. Meet the Planimal: Half Hamster Cell, Half Algae, 100% Weird

Surviving more than 150 generations of division, cells can cross vast evolutionary distances to pass on foreign genetic material.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”

Obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their new study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”

To investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

“Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga said. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”

The key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”

“Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123

On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong."

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.)

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about."

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking."

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker said.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km)

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture."

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot."

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is."

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating."

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. #6494. Why researchers are paying attention to the jolt you feel just as you drift off

A new survey links frequent sleep starts, the sudden jolts that can happen as you drift off, to poorer sleep, more severe insomnia, and greater anxiety.

Most people have felt it: the sudden jerk as sleep arrives, a leg kick or a whole-body twitch, sometimes with a falling feeling that snaps the eyes open.

In a new survey, people who reported weekly sleep starts along with at least one other symptom reported poorer sleep than those who rarely or never had them.

They also report worse insomnia, more unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and more anxiety.

The survey was online and the answers were self-reported, so it can show a pattern and not a cause. The authors wrote that the jolts and the worry may feed each other, but their data can’t say which comes first.

Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of the University of Salzburg in Austria led the work with colleagues there.

Sleep researchers call the jolt a hypnic jerk or a sleep start.

Studies that have wired people up while they doze put it in the drowsy stretch between waking and light sleep. The recordings show a brief burst of muscle activity and often a faster heartbeat.

The 96 people in the survey who had sleep starts weekly described far more than a twitch. Muscle jerks were the most common feature, reported by 87.5%.

About two-thirds described a sensation of falling or losing balance, and about the same share reported tingling or numbness.

Nearly half had felt something like an electric shock, 47.9% had seen flashes with their eyes closed, and 21.9% had heard a loud bang that wasn’t there.

Dream-like images, often of falling, went with the jolt for 74%.

The feelings that came with the jolt were mostly unpleasant. Alarm and confusion followed for about four in five participants, and panic for 71.9%. Even so, 95.8% said they usually fell back asleep quickly.

The researchers recruited 194 adults in Austria and Germany, mostly women, with an average age of about 33. Anyone reporting restless legs, sleep apnea, epilepsy or similar conditions was left out.

Ninety-six of them reported jolting awake at least weekly plus at least one other symptom. The other 98 served as the comparison group.

On standard questionnaires, the weekly group scored worse on sleep quality and on insomnia severity.

They held stronger unhelpful beliefs about sleep, rated sleep as more important to them, and scored higher on anxiety and depression.

The weekly group also took longer to fall asleep and slept slightly less.

Daytime sleepiness was the one measure that did not differ between the groups.

Within the weekly group, the people who jolted most often were the ones with the poorest sleep quality, the strongest unhelpful beliefs about sleep, and the most anxiety.

Depression scores were not linked to how often the jolts came.

Together, sleep quality, sleep beliefs, anxiety, age and gender accounted for about 27% of the differences in how often people reported sleep starts. Younger people reported them more often.

Asked what made the jolts more frequent, participants pointed to stress, tension and emotional strain. Sleep loss came up less often.

“The more strongly participants held unhelpful beliefs about sleep and the more anxious they were, the more often they reported sleep starts – and in the moment itself, many described a strong pressure to finally fall asleep,” Grünberger said.

“Our data cannot show what causes what, but this pattern resembles what we know from insomnia.”

The pressure to sleep showed up in the numbers. Among the weekly group, 83.3% said the thought “I finally have to sleep!” ran through their heads around the jolt, and 76% said they had tried to force themselves back to sleep.

Just over half of those with weekly jolts said the episodes made it harder to fall asleep. Among those who reported a delay, it averaged about 43 minutes. About 41% said the jolts made no difference.

The authors read the pattern against a well-known idea in insomnia research: the harder a person monitors and strains for sleep, the more alert they become.

In that view, the jolt and the worry about the jolt can keep each other going.

To calm the jolts, participants most often tried steering their thoughts elsewhere at bedtime, relaxation exercises, exercise, and cutting noise and light in the bedroom. They rated those as only modestly helpful.

There is no standard questionnaire for sleep starts, so the team wrote its own items from the clinical literature.

The questions have not been tested against any validated measure, and the weekly cutoff that defined the groups was chosen after the data were in.

The survey also could not separate sleep starts from look-alike experiences, such as the loud-noise phenomenon called exploding head syndrome or vivid images as sleep begins.

People answered from memory, and no one’s sleep was recorded in a lab.

“Because there is no established questionnaire for sleep starts, we developed our own items based on the clinical literature,” Grünberger said.

“This allowed us to capture a broad range of experiences – but it also means that our findings now need to be confirmed with validated instruments and objective sleep recordings.”

The next step, Schabus said, is to test whether treatments that lower arousal and sleep worry, the kind used for insomnia, also ease distressing sleep starts. No one has run that test yet.

Until someone does, the survey offers a description of the jolt and the people it troubles, and an untested idea about why.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Mental Health.

#6493. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Disease outbreaks revealed a weakened federal response

Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and New York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy says.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she said they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”

When the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli says.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” says Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the New York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm says. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a new one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”

#6490. Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

A new study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a new place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” said Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”

To study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

The messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

In human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats showed an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and says nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

About 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

The amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

To test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The new versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

Ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

The most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

The rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

The more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

People who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” said Ollmann Saphire.

Cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining showed less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

Messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

Protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

Bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

Within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group showed no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

Most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

The RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

The bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

Breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#6489. A rose-colored rock found in the Sahara turned out to be a 4.1-billion-year-old piece of Mars

A 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite found in Mali's Sahara Desert reveals clues about ancient crust, water activity and Mars' early history.

A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert formed on Mars at least 4.1 billion years ago, a study published October 29, 2026, reports.

Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, it is one of roughly 435 known meteorites from Mars, NASA says. It is also one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth.

Its composition, mineralogy and texture are distinct from those of other Martian meteorites.

Meteorite hunters found eight stones at the beginning of September 2022, weighing nearly 1.8 pounds (798.5 grams) in total.

The largest weighs about 15.6 ounces (442 grams), the Meteoritical Bulletin, the official record of named meteorites, shows.

The stones had no fusion crust, the glassy skin that forms during a fall. Their surfaces were sandblasted, and the largest pieces carried mineral coatings from burial in the desert.

At first, Teghaza 001 appeared to be a shergottite, the most common class of meteorite from Mars. It is about 50 percent pyroxene and 40 percent maskelynite, a glass formed when an impact shocks plagioclase feldspar.

Many of its pyroxene crystals have cores with thin layers of iron and manganese oxides, a product of alteration.

Oxygen isotope measurements at the University of New Mexico (UNM), which holds a 0.8-ounce (22-gram) type specimen, matched known Martian meteorites. Carl Agee, director and curator of UNM’s Institute of Meteoritics and a co-author of the study, classified the rock.

“This is just one single meteorite. It’s like going out back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop,” Agee said.

The lead author, Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, and her colleagues found tiny zircon crystals in the rock. Such crystals allow scientists to date igneous rocks with uranium-lead measurements.

A second method, in-situ rubidium-strontium dating, analyzed single mineral grains on a piece of the meteorite smaller than a fingernail. Further analysis showed when the rock formed and when changes such as water alteration occurred.

The team describes Teghaza 001 as a slowly cooled igneous rock and a sample of ancient crust. That crust formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with a primordial composition.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” Liu said.

Its exact origin can never be known for sure, but features of the rock link it to highlands in the southern hemisphere of Mars. Using data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, the researchers identified 13 locations whose mineralogy and chemistry match it.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said Lee Saper, the second author.

Saper did the research as a postdoctoral scholar at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and now works at NASA’s Ames Research Center.

Most Martian meteorites are roughly 200 million years old, according to UNM. NASA says the two other ancient ones give more limited glimpses of Mars’ geological history.

One is ALH84001, discovered in 1984 and composed almost entirely of one mineral.

A University of Houston team used lutetium-hafnium isotopes in 2010 to date it to 4.091 billion years, about 400 million years younger than earlier estimates. That age is similar to Teghaza 001’s.

The other, nicknamed “Black Beauty,” formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is made of small, volcanic rock fragments. Some of the minerals inside it are far older.

They include a 4.45 billion-year-old zircon. Scientists at Curtin University have reported that this grain preserves evidence of damage that only occurs during large meteorite impacts.

“I realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty, not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values,” Agee said of Teghaza 001.

Teghaza 001’s water-altered minerals and oxygen isotopes indicate that it reacted with fluids enriched in oxygen-18 before an impact blasted it into space. Some fine-grained carbonate, sulfate and clay minerals in the rock formed later, on Earth.

Martian water altered the rock sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, which suggests it formed even earlier, NASA said. Clues in its oxygen isotopes, texture and chemistry point to a much more dynamic water cycle on early Mars.

A June 2026 study of its water, led by Saper, had already reported the meteorite’s age and identified it as a gabbroic diorite.

Hydrogen isotopes in its phosphate minerals suggest that Martian water then held at least about twice as much deuterium, relative to hydrogen, as Earth’s seawater.

That minimum value supports models in which hydrogen escaped rapidly to space from Mars’ young atmosphere.

UNM ties the rock to the Pre-Noachian, the period from about 4.5 billion to 4.1 billion years ago.

In the Noachian that followed, until 3.7 billion years ago, groundwater chemically altered many rocks into clays, the European Space Agency notes.

The study was published in the journal Science.

#6487. Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.

An average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild. But even slightly warmer summers were linked to a higher risk of death among people with cardiovascular disease.

In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.

The risk was also higher among patients who experienced more heat waves. The odds of death rose on the hottest days and after sharp jumps in temperature from one day to the next.

Taken together, the findings indicate that heat may influence survival across entire seasons in heart patients. An influence during brief hot spells is suggested as well.

The research was conducted by Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong alongside colleagues there. Further collaborators were based at the University of Oxford.

Using health records, the investigators followed nearly 64,000 UK patients for periods of up to 16 years.

Lai said the health effects of extreme heat have “rarely been studied among people with pre-existing conditions.”

All of the patients had been enrolled in UK Biobank, a long-running British health project. Half a million volunteers aged between 37 and 73 were recruited to it from 2006 to 2010.

From this pool, 63,860 volunteers were selected by the team for analysis.

All received their first hospital diagnosis of cardiovascular disease between 2006 and 2022.

Cardiovascular disease, or CVD, includes conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels.

Four of those disorders were examined on their own as well. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, was the first of them.

The second was ischemic heart disease, in which narrowed arteries can’t deliver enough blood to the heart. Heart failure and stroke made up the remaining two.

At diagnosis, the patients had reached an average age of about 69 years. Deaths from any cause had been recorded for 12,237 of them by the end of 2022.

That figure corresponds to roughly one patient in five.

Temperature data were taken from the daily records kept by the Met Office. Those records are mapped onto squares measuring about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) across.

For every summer, defined as June through August, each home address was matched to its square.

Considerable variation in average summer temperature was evident across that map. The coldest squares averaged about 43°F (6.1°C), whereas the warmest reached about 66°F (18.7°C).

The central result relates to the average summer temperature at each patient’s place of residence. A 15% higher risk of death was associated with every additional 1.8°F (1°C).

Several other influences had been accounted for before that estimate was produced. Among them were age, sex, smoking, alcohol use, diabetes and neighborhood deprivation.

For patients with ischemic heart disease, each added degree Celsius corresponded to a 19% higher risk. A smaller increase of 10% was found among those with atrial fibrillation.

The results for heart failure and stroke were less certain. In both groups, the link with average summer temperature was too weak to exclude chance.

Adults aged 65 and older in New England had been examined in an earlier US study.

A 1% increase in deaths was reported there for each 1.8°F (1°C) rise in long-term average summer temperature. Older adults in general were covered by that work, not only people with heart disease.

Heat waves were also counted by the researchers. A heat wave was defined as two or more consecutive days hotter than 90% of local summer days.

Exposure to four or more heat waves a year was experienced by some patients. Their risk of death exceeded by 24% that of patients exposed to two or fewer.

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the corresponding increase in risk was 29%. It stood at 28% among those with heart failure.

A second analysis was restricted to patients whose deaths occurred during a summer.

For each such patient, temperatures on the day of death and the five preceding days were examined. These were then compared with other days in the same month that fell on the same weekday.

Because every patient served as their own comparison, fixed traits can’t account for the results. Sex and schooling are examples of such traits.

On the hottest 1% of summer days, the odds of death among the patients as a group were 70% higher. The reference point was the temperature at which deaths were lowest.

Temperature changes from one day to the next were measured as well. The largest one-day rises were taken to be those in the top 1% of such changes.

After rises of that size, the odds of death were roughly double those seen when temperature held constant.

Roughly threefold odds were found in patients with ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

Considerable uncertainty surrounds the estimates for sharp rises. In heart failure, the plausible range extended from 36% higher odds to more than seven times as high.

No clear link with deaths was detected for sudden drops in temperature.

Events inside the patients’ bodies were not measured at any point in the study. A plausible explanation was instead drawn by the authors from earlier research on extreme heat.

In hot weather, warm blood is pumped toward the skin so that heat can be shed by the body. As much as 5 gallons (20 liters) of blood may be pumped by the heart each minute.

Sweating can meanwhile strip water and salt from the body. Blood that holds less water becomes thicker, and thicker blood may clot more readily.

In a person with heart disease, the extra pumping may require more oxygen than the heart can obtain.

Among patients lacking a college or university degree, warmer summers were tied more strongly to death. A weaker link was seen in patients who held such a degree.

A similar contrast emerged between neighborhoods with moderate green space and the greenest neighborhoods, where the link was weaker.

Among heart failure patients, the link was stronger in the most deprived neighborhoods.

Several possible reasons were put forward by the authors. Deprived neighborhoods tend to be overcrowded and to suffer more air pollution and traffic noise, they wrote.

Physically demanding work in extreme weather is also more common among people with less money.

Green spaces, meanwhile, have been shown in earlier studies to cool their surroundings.

According to Lai, protection will have to be delivered at several levels at once. City planning was named as one of those levels.

Cooling strategies form another, as do personal decisions about where to live. Lai said such protection is needed most by the most vulnerable groups.

Extreme heat is projected to grow more frequent and more intense as populations age. That observation came from study co-author Chinmoy Sarkar of the University of Hong Kong.

Together, he said, those trends will make protecting frail people with chronic diseases a top public health priority.

A link between heat and death can be demonstrated by a study of this kind. Proof that heat caused the deaths lies beyond its reach.

Because temperatures were assigned by home address, the patients’ actual whereabouts each day remain unrecorded. Nor was any information available on air-conditioning use or on changes in medication.

Smoking and drinking habits were recorded only once, when volunteers joined UK Biobank.

Those habits may well have changed afterward. Since cases were identified through hospital admissions, milder disease that never led to admission was missed.

UK Biobank volunteers may also differ from the wider population. About 96% of the patients in this study were white. The authors wrote that the volunteers may not represent everyone in the UK with cardiovascular disease.

None of the patients was given a cooler home or a greener street during the study. How many deaths such changes might prevent therefore can’t be read from the records.

Air-conditioning use could be accounted for in future research, as could travel to places with different temperatures.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.
