Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

#6485. Ice baths after exercise: What happens when you make them a habit?

Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.

An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness. But taking one after every lifting session may make it harder to build muscle and strength over time.

A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.

Researchers analyzed 15 published systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Together they covered 161 studies and more than 3,200 participants.

The takeaway is simple. Athletes, coaches, and fitness fans should be strategic, not habitual, with ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool,” said lead author Erfan Berjisian, a PhD student at ECU.

“Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete’s goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled.”

The review found ice baths are particularly good at reducing muscle soreness. They also lower markers of muscle damage and they help athletes feel recovered faster.

Muscle soreness dropped consistently for up to four days after exercise. Markers of muscle damage were lower between 24 and 72 hours after an ice bath.

The review also noted a boost in heart rate variability right after exercise. That’s a sign the body is starting to recover.

For athletes who need to compete again soon, the benefits depend on what they’ll be doing and how much time they have to recover.

“Cold-water immersion appears especially useful when recovery time is limited, such as during tournaments, congested competition schedules or repeated high-intensity training sessions,” Berjisian said.

Researchers found endurance performance improved within the first hour after an ice bath. Power and jump performance often improved 24 to 72 hours later.

However, explosive performance actually dropped in the hours right after an ice bath.

That likely happens due to the temporary cooling effect on muscles.

“If athletes need to perform high-speed or explosive movements soon after cooling, cold-water immersion may be counterproductive unless sufficient re-warming occurs,” said co-author Kristina Kendall from ECU.

Perhaps the most significant finding was about repeated use.

Athletes who constantly used cold-water immersion after resistance training saw smaller improvements in strength, muscle size, and power.

The evidence suggests chronic use may blunt some of the body’s normal muscle-building responses to training.

The review also found a detail worth noting. The effect on strength may depend on the protocol.

Immersing just the exercised limb was linked to reduced gains. Whole-body immersion showed no clear detrimental effect.

For endurance athletes, it  was a different story. The review found no evidence that regular cold-water immersion harmed aerobic fitness or endurance adaptations.

The results suggest that cold-water immersion at 50–59°F (10–15°C) for 10–15 minutes generally helped with post-workout recovery.

Colder water, at 41–50°F (5–10°C) for the same duration, may help restore jumping performance and lower markers of muscle damage.

Both intermittent and continuous protocols worked, with no clear winner between them.

The authors also assessed the quality of that evidence. They rated it low to very low.

Most of the samples were male, which limits how well the findings apply to women.

The authors also flagged some overlap between the reviews, especially the ones on strength and muscle growth. Those conclusions rest on a fairly concentrated group of trials.

The review calls for more work on women and on different training types. It also wants research that tracks athletes over longer periods.

Ice baths may ease soreness when athletes have limited time to recover, and their effects on performance vary with the activity and the timing.

But the science says athletes should stop treating them as a cure-all.

They should be more cautious when the goal is building strength and muscle mass.

When races or matches are only a day or two apart, an ice bath may ease soreness before the next event. That can matter during a tournament, when athletes have little time to recover between rounds.

If your goal is to build muscle or get stronger, consider saving the cold plunge for competition days.

Making it a routine after lifting may limit the gains you’re training for.

The study is published in the journal Sports Medicine – Open.

#6483. Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A star called “Little Bao” danced with its giant partner “Big Bao”

An image captured by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) telescope shows the Andromeda galaxy, which is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way — and the home galaxy of Big and Little Bao.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

#6482. Male bumblebees usually leave the nest, so what happens when they stay?

Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.

In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.

The queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young. Males are expected to leave soon after reaching adulthood, mate and then die.

A new study of lab-reared common eastern bumblebees has now found males helping with the young. The developing brood was warmed by the males with their own body heat.

Queens housed with males laid eggs sooner. After 28 days, nests with five males contained about 49 eggs, larvae and pupae on average, compared with 33 in nests with a queen alone.

The experiments were run by Meghan Moore and Hollis Woodard at the University of California, Riverside. Both are entomologists. Their nests were not natural ones.

Queens were housed with as many as five males and no workers, a mix rarely seen in the wild.

The project began with photos taken for a different experiment. Moore had pointed a thermal camera at the nests. Bright white patches of heat showed up on the males.

Bumblebees raise their eggs, larvae and pupae together in a single clump. Biologists call these young the brood. A queen keeps the brood warm much as a hen warms her eggs.

She straddles the clump and presses her abdomen against it. The heat is produced by muscles in her thorax, the middle part of her body.

This posture was first described in 1972 for another bumblebee species.

On each of 12 days, every nest was photographed four times within one hour. In total, 2,304 usable thermal images were collected.

The images were labeled so that scorers could not tell which kind of nest each one showed.

Males in the queen’s posture turned out to be hot. Their thoraxes averaged 94.6°F (34.8°C). Males standing on the brood without that posture averaged about 88°F (31°C).

Queens in the same posture averaged about 99°F (37.2°C). The males were not simply resting on a warm spot. Heat was being made in their bodies the way a queen makes it, only less of it.

Heat generated in the thorax is passed back to the abdomen. That rear section is the part a bee presses against the brood. Here, too, queens and males behaved differently.

In incubating queens, the abdomen was about 2.9°F (1.6°C) cooler than the thorax. In incubating males, the abdomen was 6.7°F (3.7°C) cooler. Their gap was more than twice as wide.

A possible reason was offered by the authors, who described it as speculation. Heat is known to damage sperm, including in males of another bumblebee species.

By limiting the heat that reaches his abdomen, a male may protect his sperm.

No sperm were examined in this study. For now the idea remains untested.

Moore and Woodard began the nest experiment with 75 mated queens. Each queen had been treated with carbon dioxide. This let her skip winter dormancy and begin laying eggs.

Some queens were given a nest box to themselves. Others shared a box with one, three or five young males from other colonies.

Queens living alone needed about 15 days to lay their first eggs. With one male, the wait dropped to about 11 days. It fell to about eight days with three males and about six with five.

A queen with five males therefore started laying in less than half the time of a lone queen.

Every nest was then allowed 28 days to grow, counted from its first eggs. An earlier start on egg laying could not explain a bigger nest at the end.

Fifteen queens died before the experiment was over. The brood counts come from the nests that remained.

After those 28 days, nests of lone queens held about 33 eggs, larvae and pupae on average.

Nests with five males held about 49. That is roughly 1.5 times as many. Nests with one or three males fell in between.

Only the nests with five males produced more adult workers during that time. They averaged about five workers per nest. The other groups averaged two or three.

Queens were photographed incubating about as often whether or not males were present.

The photos also showed fewer instances in which no bee was incubating the brood when males were present.

Incubation helps maintain nest temperatures, which in turn support the brood’s development. Where males were photographed incubating more often, more older brood was found at the end.

According to the authors, male incubation may directly support the growth of the brood. They also wrote that more work is needed to show cause.

Nests holding males but no workers are unusual. For that reason a smaller test was also run. Five nests containing both males and worker bees were filmed for 24 hours in darkness with infrared cameras.

Males incubated in all five nests. Two of the nests were young, with fewer than 15 bees. Two others were mature, with 50 or more.

On video, a male can be picked out by a patch of facial hair. It is sometimes described as a moustache.

Male incubation is not a new observation.

In 1985, entomologist Sydney Cameron reported that males of a different bumblebee species incubate pupae. Moore and Woodard have now added a second species.

They also measured how nests developed when males were present.

How often males do any of this in wild nests cannot yet be said. Young wild nests usually hold a queen and her workers. Males mostly appear late in the season.

The lab males were also unable to leave. Any male inclined to fly off had no way to do so. The authors wrote that this may have made the males more likely to incubate.

The bees came from commercially reared colonies, which may behave differently from wild ones. They were also given food instead of foraging for it.

Wild bumblebee nests are hard to find. As a result, data on wild colonies that produce males early are scarce.

Incubation takes a great deal of energy. What that work costs a male, in energy or in fertility, was not measured.

“What’s the trade-off? There’s no free lunch,” Woodard said.

Further studies are planned on whether caring for brood affects the males’ bodies. Future research will also need to test whether male incubation itself makes nests grow. Its importance in wild colonies is still unknown.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6481. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6479. What makes artwork memorable? Artists put their instincts to the test

Artists found that making forgettable artwork was harder than making memorable pieces, while AI predicted viewers' memories better.

Could you make a painting that someone would look at and forget minutes later?

In an art contest, researchers gave artists a choice: Create something viewers would remember or something they would quickly forget.

In a recognition test, entries meant to be memorable were recognized more often than entries meant to be forgettable.

The memorable entries also came closer to the researchers’ target for their category.

A computer model called ResMem, trained on photographs, was better than artists and a separate group of raters at sorting the most- and least-remembered artworks.

Trent Davis and Yifei Chen carried out the study together with Wilma Bainbridge of the University of Chicago.

Bainbridge leads the Brain Bridge Lab there and is an associate professor in the Department of Psychology.

Memory was tested within minutes of the art having been seen in every part of the study.

For three months the art contest remained open to adult artists who lived in the continental United States.

Each of them was permitted to enter a single piece and had to choose a category for it. Memorable and forgettable were the two categories on offer and an artist could not enter both.

The organizers accepted only flat physical works, of which paintings, drawings, and collages are examples. Digital art and photography had been excluded under the rules that the team had drawn up.

In all, 144 submissions were received from 20 states and 86 of them met the rules. Of those 86 artworks, 62 had been entered as memorable and the other 24 as forgettable.

The first memory test was completed online by a group of 119 adults who were living in the United States. All 86 of the artworks were presented to these viewers one after another in a single long stream.

Some of the artworks were shown for a second time once at least 30 seconds had passed. The viewers had been instructed to press a key whenever they believed that an artwork had appeared before.

A score for every artwork in the contest was then worked out by the team from those key presses.

Mean scores of 0.86 and 0.79 out of 1 were obtained for memorable and forgettable entries respectively. Although modest in size, this difference was unlikely to be attributable to chance.

A high target score had been set by the team for memorable entries and a low one for forgettable entries.

It was found that the memorable entries had come closer to their target than the forgettable entries had.

The team then selected the works that had been remembered best and worst by the online viewers.

Thirty-nine of those works were shown for a month at Connect Gallery in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago.

Sixty-two visitors walked through the show and were free to look at the works in whatever order they wished. They had been informed that memory was the theme of the show but not that a test would follow.

Recognition was assessed afterward in a separate room where artworks were presented to the visitors on their own phones.

A mean of 89% of the tested visitors recognized any given piece from the best-remembered group. The corresponding proportion for pieces from the least-remembered group was 70% of the visitors.

Bainbridge called the show a risky experiment for the lab. Visitors to a small exhibition about memory had been given a reason to try to remember each of the pieces.

Works from the two groups had for the most part been hung on opposite walls of the gallery.

The test was therefore repeated with 141 people at a vision science conference where paper prints were mixed together.

The works remembered best online were again recognized more often than the works that had been remembered least.

The artworks were also rated on 21 qualities by a separate group of 892 people. One of those qualities was the degree to which each artwork seemed memorable to the person rating it.

The works described as memorable by these raters were not reliably the ones remembered by online viewers. It was the goals chosen by the artists that the ratings were instead found to match.

Higher memorability ratings were given to art that people found complex, surprising, interesting, or likely to become famous.

The works that viewers tended to remember were those that raters felt able to rebuild easily in the mind. Works in which a person was shown were also remembered better whereas landscapes were remembered worse.

Works that looked digitally made were remembered better too. Every entry in the contest had nevertheless been made by hand.

“What people think is memorable is different from what actually is,” Chen said.

ResMem is a neural network, which is a kind of AI program that learns from examples. It was built in Bainbridge’s lab and was trained on nearly 70,000 photographs.

The model takes in an image and returns a score that shows how likely people are to remember it.

In an earlier study, memory for more than 4,000 paintings from the Art Institute of Chicago was predicted by ResMem.

The researchers compared three ways of predicting which artworks people would remember. They looked at the 20 most remembered and the 20 least remembered pieces.

The AI model, ResMem, correctly sorted 80% of the 40 artworks. The artists’ own choices were correct 67.5% of the time.

The separate group’s ratings correctly classified 62.5% of the artworks.

ResMem also predicted which artworks gallery visitors would remember. People’s ratings could not do this reliably.

The researchers think the AI model may perform better because it does not judge art the way people do. For example, people may assume that interesting or surprising art is easier to remember, even when that is not true.

The study did not explain why making memorable art was easier than making forgettable art.

Researchers think memorable images may share certain features that catch people’s attention. Forgettable images may not have anything in common, making them harder to create on purpose.

Artists chose whether to enter the contest and which category to compete in. Some had taught themselves to make art, while others had master’s degrees in fine arts.

Neither education nor professional experience clearly affected their success. However, the researchers had only basic information about their training.

Gallery visitors may also have been more interested in art than the people who took the online test.

The researchers want to study more highly trained artists. They also suggest tracking where people look in a gallery to better understand which artworks stay in their memory.

The full study was published in the journal Psychological Science.

#6476. Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

Cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in. A new study found that growing roots release oxygen even at night.

The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud. To keep these roots alive, the plant carries air down from its leaves.

Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.

It has generally been assumed that this leak occurs mostly in daylight. During the day, the leaves produce oxygen and their pores stay open to the air.

A laboratory study of narrowleaf cattails has found that daylight altered the leak only slightly. Instead, oxygen appeared wherever a new root or underground stem was growing. It remained there through the night as well.

The findings suggest that the season of root growth may matter more for marsh chemistry than the time of day.

The study was conducted by Ilana Stein and Zoe Cardon of the Ecosystems Center. This center is part of the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

Four plants were examined one at a time in boxes of marsh mud. No measurements were made in a marsh itself.

Flooding leaves the soil of a wetland without oxygen. Most wetland plants cope with this through spongy tissue in their leaves, stems and roots that is filled with air.

This tissue serves as a kind of snorkel for the plant. Oxygen travels through it from the air above the water to the root tips below.

Narrowleaf cattail is particularly well adapted to flooded ground. Air spaces were found by earlier studies to make up as much as 74% of its leaf tissue.

In the roots, the figure reached as much as 32%.

Some of the oxygen that arrives is used by the roots and the rest can leak away. This leaked oxygen allows microbes that depend on it to survive in mud where they otherwise could not.

Certain microbes consume methane before the gas can enter the plant and escape through its leaves. Others break down organic matter in the mud and could reduce how much carbon the soil stores.

The same leak is also valuable to people. Cattails are planted in constructed wetlands that treat wastewater and are used to clean up contaminated soil. Both of these uses rely on the oxygen released by their roots.

Cattails and mud were collected by Stein and Cardon from a marsh along the Parker River in northeastern Massachusetts. This marsh forms part of the Plum Island Ecosystems Long Term Ecological Research program.

Each plant was placed in a narrow clear plastic box filled with live mud from the same marsh. The box measured about 15.5 inches tall and 8 inches wide (39 by 20 centimeters).

Much of one inside wall was covered with a film containing a dye that responds to oxygen. A camera photographed the film under blue light.

The colors in every image indicated how much oxygen was present in the mud behind the film.

These films were made by hand by Suzanne Thomas, who works as a senior research assistant at MBL.

Images were captured every few minutes over periods that usually lasted two to three days.

The box itself remained in darkness behind black cloth. Meanwhile, the leaves grew outside under a lamp that was switched on from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.

A sensor attached to one leaf collected readings once every minute. It recorded how quickly the leaf absorbed carbon dioxide and how widely its pores had opened.

The team could therefore compare the activity of the leaves with the oxygen in the mud.

Mud that held no roots also held no oxygen. This changed as soon as part of a cattail grew into it.

Cattails spread by means of horizontal underground stems known as rhizomes. New roots then emerge from these stems.

Whenever a new rhizome or root entered a patch of mud, the oxygen level there rose rapidly from zero. It climbed to between 25% and 35% of the amount found in water that is fully saturated with air.

This oxygen did not persist for long. Around a rhizome, it disappeared after about three days on average. Around a main root, it lasted about four days.

According to the authors, a seal may be partly responsible. Older sections of a cattail root develop a barrier that is thought to keep oxygen inside. This would allow more of it to reach the growing tip.

Stein and Cardon wrote that this barrier and the steady demand for oxygen in the mud may explain the decline.

In many cases, oxygen returned to the mud a second time. Fine side roots broke through the sealed surface of a main root and oxygen spread through the mud around them.

These later pools of oxygen persisted for about three weeks on average. In one plant, they lasted longer than five weeks.

An earlier study had found that cattail side roots do not develop the barrier that seals a main root.

As a result, a single root released oxygen into the mud on two occasions. The first release lasted a few days near the tip and the second continued for weeks along the sides.

Earlier studies of rice and a salt marsh cordgrass had reported strong control of the leak by day and night. In the cattails, light did have some effect and this was mostly seen around the side roots.

Across three plants, the gap between the highest and lowest oxygen levels of each day averaged about 3% of saturation. No daily pattern could be detected in the fourth plant.

New growth therefore changed oxygen levels far more than the cycle of day and night.

The oxygen in the mud also did not follow the activity of the leaves. It increased during the first two to three hours of light. For the rest of the day, it declined even though the leaves were becoming more active.

After the lights were turned off, the oxygen fell for about two hours. It then rose slowly until the following morning.

Mud consumes oxygen quickly on its own. Oxygen-rich water was injected into mud that held no roots. The oxygen was gone within about an hour and a half.

The roots must therefore have continued to release oxygen in the dark.

The authors wrote that it remains unclear how cattails achieve this without exhausting the oxygen in their own air spaces.

One explanation they proposed is that the leaf pores did not close completely at night. Air could then have continued to enter the plant.

Methane, soil carbon, and microbes were not examined in the study.

The study also followed just four plants of a single species. None of them was kept in its box for more than two months.

If growth is what controls the oxygen, then the next question is when cattails grow underground.

Stein is a postdoctoral researcher in Cardon’s lab. She said the results turned the team’s attention to the timing of root growth across the year.

Earlier field data and models suggest that cattail rhizomes gain the most mass in mid to late summer. This follows the expansion of the leaves.

The authors wrote that oxygen from new rhizomes and their roots may be especially intense during that period.

Methane is released by wetlands naturally and oxygen around roots can reduce it.

“Natural greenhouse gas emissions have been happening forever,” said Cardon, a senior scientist at MBL.

She said the team hopes to identify natural processes that could act as levers on those emissions.

The cattails were not followed through a complete growing season or observed in a marsh. The authors wrote that understanding when rhizomes and roots grow through the year should become a priority.

In their view, such knowledge is needed to understand the chemistry of marshes where cattails dominate.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#6474. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6473. Some patients who appear unresponsive can control a computer with their thoughts

One in three ICU patients who appeared comatose changed a beeping tone by thinking, and that sign of hidden consciousness predicted recovery.

After a severe brain injury, a patient may show no visible response when doctors ask them to move. But their brain waves can sometimes reveal that they’re following the command.

In a New York intensive care unit, 13 of 41 patients who appeared unresponsive changed how fast a sound beeped by trying to open and close a hand.

Electrodes on the scalp recorded the patients’ brain waves. A bedside computer detected signals linked to the attempted movement and adjusted the beeping the patients heard through headphones.

The 13 who could do it were also far more likely to regain consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, they were far more likely to be able to look after themselves for hours at a time.

Jan Claassen, a professor of neurology at Columbia University’s Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, led the study.

He also runs the neurocritical care unit at NewYork-Presbyterian and Columbia University Irving Medical Center, where the patients were treated.

In a 2019 study, his team recorded brain waves while unresponsive patients were told to open and close a hand. A computer program found that about 15% of them were trying to comply.

Some patients showed brain activity consistent with following a command even though they did not visibly move. Researchers call this cognitive motor dissociation.

“Our brain-computer interface is only a first step, but it shows that, in principle, we could hopefully in the future give some of these patients a voice,” Claassen said.

Most brain-computer interfaces that let paralyzed people type, play games, or move a robotic arm use a chip implanted on the brain, and they need long training.

Neither suits someone who was healthy last week and isn’t responding now.

So the team used the 21 EEG electrodes already glued to each patient’s scalp.

Through headphones, a recorded voice said “to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand,” then “to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand.”

A bedside computer read the brain waves as they came in and changed the beeps when it detected the effort.

Each session was two five-minute practice rounds, during which the program learned that patient’s signals, and then a ten-minute test with no help.

The voice encouraged patients when the beeps changed and congratulated them when they hit the target.

The 41 patients were tested a median of five days after their injuries. Their median age was 65, and most had suffered a stroke, a brain bleed, a cardiac arrest, or a head injury.

Thirteen of the 41 patients, or 32%, passed the test on at least one try. Six of them did it within the first week after their injury, which surprised the researchers.

For comparison, all eight healthy volunteers controlled the tone, and so did nine of 22 conscious patients in the same unit. The conscious patients who failed were mostly sedated, agitated, or unable to speak after a stroke.

The unresponsive patients who succeeded were slow. Their brain signals showed up about 50 seconds after each instruction.

Conscious patients took about 17 seconds and healthy volunteers about 15. A patient who looks like they are ignoring a command may simply be answering it late.

Each patient also took the team’s older command-following exam, the one from 2019. Eight of the 41 passed it. Every one of those who was tested on the tone the same day could control it.

But nine of the 33 patients who failed the older exam could control the tone anyway.

The authors wrote that the beeping feedback may simply be more engaging than a voice repeating the same command.

“EEG is used in clinical practice every day in the ICU,” Claassen said.

“The only sophisticated part is the computer program we wrote, which analyzes the data in real time and modulates the feedback to the patient.”

Four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone regained consciousness before leaving the hospital.

Among the 28 patients who could not control the beeping, only one had regained consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, six of the 13, or 46%, could be left alone for at least eight hours a day without help. Two of the 28 others, or 7%, could. Patients who had failed both tests did worst of all.

Of those 24 patients, not one recovered that much. By then 17 of the 41 had died, 14 of them after life support was withdrawn.

The deaths after withdrawal are why the authors wrote at length about ethics.

Four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone died after life support was withdrawn. The authors cautioned that a negative result cannot rule out awareness.

The study covered one hospital and 41 patients with very different injuries, some of them sedated during testing.

Patients who recovered were also examined more often, which could have made recovery easier to spot in them. The authors wrote that the result needs repeating at other centers before it guides care.

Controlling a tone is also not talking. The study didn’t try to get a yes or a no from anyone. The authors wrote that doing so may need a level of awareness beyond what this test detects.

Families and the conscious patients were asked what they wanted.

All 37 who answered supported the idea, and they asked for a loved one’s voice in place of the recording, and for ways to signal pain, hunger, or simple awareness.

“Our goal is to refine the system so that patients can tell their doctors and loved ones how they are feeling – if they are in pain or hungry, for instance – with more direct communication,” Claassen said.

For some patients who showed no visible response at the bedside, the beeps offered evidence that they could follow a command.

The full study was published in the journal Brain.

Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years.

The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky.

Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA.

However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging.

Jupiter's Trojans are the most famous; the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center notes that an incredible 15,000 of these objects have been discovered so far. But some other planets, including Neptune, also host Trojans. In fact, a 2005 study suggested that Neptune has up to 10 times more Trojans than Jupiter. Until now, though, astronomers have spotted only 28 Neptunian Trojans, with just two of these being long-term L5 members.

There are two reasons why it's difficult to detect these rocks. First, the Neptunian Trojans are extremely faint. More critically, for nearly 15 years, the Trojan population's position in the sky relative to Earth has overlapped with the central region of the Milky Way. Consequently, bright background stars have made it nearly impossible to discern the tiny, faint asteroids, Megan Schwamb, the study's first author and a researcher who focuses on how planets and their building blocks form and evolve at Queen's University Belfast, told Live Science in an email.

An illustration of the Jovian Trojans orbiting in front of and behind Jupiter

However, from 2025 onward, the L5 group's position has moved — albeit extremely slowly — away from the galactic plane. This has made the population slightly easier to observe. At the same time, the Rubin Observatory started scanning the entire Southern Hemisphere sky with the world's largest digital camera.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Rubin is pretty uniquely suited to being excellent at discovering Neptune Trojans," study co-author Kathryn Volk, a scientist at the Planetary Science Institute in Arizona, told Live Science in an email. "The on-sky density of these objects is not particularly high, so having a large field of view helps a lot!" (Rubin has a field of view equivalent to seven full moons, according to the observatory's website.) This, along with the observatory's excellent vision — which allows it to detect objects 100 billion times dimmer than Venus — enabled the discovery of the new Trojans.

The new Trojan observations form part of the Rubin Science Validation Survey, a three-month-long test run that was held in mid-2025 prior to the start of the observatory's flagship decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which is now underway. By chance, the Science Validation Survey encompassed the part of the sky containing Neptune's L5 Trojans, leading to the asteroids being photographed within three weeks of the survey's start.

Following the discoveries, the researchers created computer models to determine the asteroids' orbits. These simulations revealed that the duo will continue to tag behind Neptune for a billion years. The results suggest that the asteroids' trajectories have been stable for several billion years, which means the asteroids may have been traversing these routes from the time of the early solar system. The researchers also found a third object in Rubin's data, but it had a stable orbit in only some of their simulations, leading them to classify it as a candidate Trojan rather than a confirmed one.

However, the two confirmed Trojans likely didn't form in place alongside Neptune. The simulations showed that the asteroids' orbits are highly tilted, just like those of the previously discovered L5 asteroids — suggesting that Neptune captured these objects as they were hurtling past.

Determining the properties of both the Jovian and Neptunian Trojan asteroids will help researchers understand what happened during the solar system's infancy, when the giant planets are believed to have migrated to their present-day positions, Volk said.

Schwamb expects the LSST to unveil many more of the hypothesized Neptunian Trojans, especially because it will survey this same patch of the sky repeatedly over the next several months.

Schwamb, M. E., Bernardinelli, P. H., Volk, K., Murtagh, J., 林 H. W. 省. L., Rivkin, A. S., Chandler, C. O., Jones, R. L., Benecchi, S. D., Jurić, M., Kurlander, J. A., Greenstreet, S., Wilson, A., West, M., & Lyttle, R. R. (2026). NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s first view of the Neptune Trojan L5 (Trailing) cloud: Two new long-term stable Trojans. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1010(2), L36. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aead9a
