#6461. The 7 Best Robot Vacuums Withstood Every Mess We Threw at Them

We scattered crumbs, dust, and debris to determine which models could power through these piles of mess without a hiccup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

They’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

Below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

For models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

In each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

To better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

Our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

We are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As new components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

We’ll soon be testing the Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum, which is an uprgraded version of our previous Best Overall recommendation, the Qrevo S. The latest model offers much of the same functionality, along with a few improvements—and a couple trade-offs.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. The spinning mop heads reach 200 rotations per minute and lift 10 millimeters, helping prevent carpets and area rugs from getting wet as the robot vacuum moves between thresholds. However, unlike the Qrevo S, the mop heads rely on air drying rather than using a hot air drying system, which could mean longer downtime between cleaning sessions.

Beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor plans, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

To support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

If you–or your pet–tend to shed a lot of hair, the Eureka J15 Pro robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. The base has a built-in, automatic hair cutting tool that slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have manually remove hair from the roller.

This robot vacuum isn’t lacking in power, either. It delivers 16,000 Pa suction for a deeper clean, and it works on a variety of floor types like carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile. The J15 Pro has advanced obstacle detection, and our tester, who has been using this model for months, tells us that it’s great at avoiding furniture, cords, pet toys, and over-friendly pets. It even takes a picture whenever it runs into something in its cleaning path, and you’re able to view the photo within the map afterwards in case it’s something that should be moved liked shoes and cords (or an animal).

The mopping feature is also effective at keeping your house clean. There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper clean, and they extend to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards. Our tester found the J15 Pro to be quiet on all modes, but Turbo is noticeably louder than the nighttime mode. You have control over suction power, though, so it doesn’t have to be running at full capacity constantly if you want to cut down on background noise.

She does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. There are a plethora of settings and options available, and while it’s easy to set up basic settings initially, it gets a lot more involved. Those who are really just looking for daily maintenance and don’t want all the bells and whistles may find this cumbersome.

As a first-time robot vacuum owner, our tester has been very pleased with his ongoing experience using the dreame X40 Ultra. It’s been able to take on dirt, dust, crumbs, and anything that his dog tracks inside, and exceeded expectations on hardwood floors. There are a few places it struggled to reach, like under a coffee table and TV stand, but we chalk that up to a height issue rather than capability concerns.

The X40 Ultra has 12,000 Pa of suction power, and a liftable, extendable side brush that gets close to wall corners and furniture legs. To protect rugs and carpets from getting wet, the robot vacuum either detaches the mop heads or lifts them to 10.5 millimeters, preventing any wet and dry mess combinations.

The app also allows you to program no-go zones, including rugs or other problem areas like staircases. Even with pet toys laying around the house, the X40 was able to navigate and map the layout with ease, all while avoiding these obstacles.

The mopping feature is a favorite for our tester. If you’re constantly on the go, having a robot vacuum capable of mopping on a daily basis is a real game changer. And thanks to auto-empty and auto-refill tanks, it’s really a set-it-and-forget-it device. We only suggest that you run the robot vacuum overnight so you aren’t disturbed by its run cycle. (Waking up to beautiful, clean floors is fun, too.)

Full Dreame X40 Ultra Robotic Vacuum Review

Ecovacs has been around since the late 90’s, and the brand introduced its first Deebot in 2007. Needless to say, its designs have come along way, and one of the latest versions piqued our interest for one main reason: stain removal.

Most often, robot vacuums with mopping capability can only handle fresh spills on hardwood and tile, not the stubborn, dried-on stuff. The Deebot X12 is trying to change that. It uses an AI camera and infrared stain detector to identify spills, splatters, and even muddy paw prints. Then, it deploys two jets with cleaning solution at up to 46,000 Pascals to loosen residue for the mop roller head to pick up. This could potentially save you from having to make a more detailed pass by hand.

The vacuum has capable power on carpet, too. It uses 22,000 Pascals of suction power to get rid or dirt, hair, and debris, and features an anti-tangle side and main brush to prevent hair from getting trapped around the bristles and roller.

The docking station is one of the more advanced designs we’ve seen in a robot vacuum. It has a bagless dustbin, power washing for the mop roller, and hot air drying. We’re looking forward to testing out this model and updating this guide accordingly with our findings.

Full Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicycle Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

The Qrevo CurvX is a newer design from Roborock, and we like that is has a slimmer build to fit under a wider variety of furniture, but still packs 22,000 Pa of suction power (the highest on our list). It’s equipped with a range of smart features, including pet recognition technology and two-way video calling (in the Roborock app) to interact with furry friends while you’re away, making it a great choice for households with animals.

The initial mapping process took a bit of time, but alas, this is a crucial step for an accurate layout of your home. Once the mapping was complete, the CurvX navigated efficiently, avoiding unnecessary paths and cleaning strategically as it went. During operation, the vacuum ran very quietly, especially when compared to other Roborock models we’ve experienced.

One of the biggest conveniences is the automatic dustbin emptying system, as it significantly reduces the need for manual maintenance. The tanks hold debris for up to seven weeks, and the water tank automatically refills the reservoir on the robot vacuum so you don’t have to.

The mop lifting and carpet detection performed well in our lab tests. When used in the concrete floor pen with obstacles like a small rug, it raised the heads with ease when transitioning between floor types. This ensured that carpets didn’t get wet during mopping sessions and the robot maintained the right cleaning mode. The edge mopping system is also a fantastic feature. The mop heads sit on arms that extend outwards for better reach, and they were able to get under and around table legs more efficiently.

That being said, this model isn’t without its limitations. In some of our mess tests, it missed detritus that was close to the pen walls, or “room edges,” despite the side brush kicking up the debris. It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Full Roborock Qrevo CruvX Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

If you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

The vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

One of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

Many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:

Eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

Roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

This navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

With this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM)

This triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each new model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for big homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

The most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

Throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

When set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

For homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

#6460. What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.

A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk. Could a computer start from scratch and recognize many of those same words on roughly the same timetable?

Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.

The researchers turned speech recorded around eight children into clean audio using synthetic voices.

They trained a separate model on each child’s audio in the order the speech was originally recorded.

The models identified recurring sound patterns that corresponded to words.

On average, each model reached the halfway point on a vocabulary checklist within 22 days of the child it was paired with.

“We wanted to turn the usual logic of developmental research around,” said Uri Hasson, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Princeton who led the study.

“Instead of observing a child for an hour in the laboratory, we asked whether we could build a model capable of learning and immerse it in the child’s actual experience, day after day.”

The families were in New Jersey and spanned a range of incomes and backgrounds. Each home got four to 14 recording devices spread across two to five rooms.

The devices ran 12 to 14 hours a day, from February 2022 to May 2025.

The project gathered roughly 1.2 million hours of audio and video, of which the eight homes analyzed in this paper supplied about 600,000. An automated pipeline worked out where the child was in the house and pulled out the speech happening nearby.

Each child ended up with between 1,900 and 6,600 hours of usable speech, three to seven and a half hours a day. That adds up to 6 to 27 million words per child, over a median of 960 recording days.

Every month from eight months on, caregivers filled out a standard checklist of which words their child understood and said. Those forms are how the researchers knew what each child knew, and when.

Children reached half of the 649-word checklist anywhere from about 12 to 22 months old. That ten-month spread between children is the thing most studies average away.

The model started from random numbers. It had no dictionary, no phonetics, no notion of where one word ends and the next begins, and no text.

The program’s first part chops the incoming sound into 20-millisecond pieces and sorts them into categories it invents for itself. Its second part tries to guess the next piece from what came before.

Whenever a run of pieces becomes reliably predictable, the program files it away as a unit, which is the closest thing it has to a word.

Nothing about that design is specific to English or even to speech. What makes it unusual is the schedule.

The audio arrives in the order it was recorded, one day at a time, rather than shuffled into batches the way an AI language model is normally trained.

At the end of each simulated day, the program gets a sample of speech from earlier days, weighted toward recent ones. The researchers call it replay.

English has 39 phonemes, the sound units that distinguish bat from pat. Children spend their first year tuning in to the ones their own language uses.

Within roughly 12 to 15 months of simulated time, the program had carved out dedicated categories for nearly all of them.

Across the eight children, the models averaged 37.5 phonemes each. The lowest count came from the household with the least recording.

The order it happened in, sounds before words, is the order infants follow.

Words came after. For the child the paper calls Coral, the checklist said she understood 97 words at 12 months, and her model had 91.

Across all eight children, the models and the children hit the same vocabulary milestones within an average of 22 days of each other, with the worst case 56 days.

The models also reproduced the differences between children, landing close to each child’s own halfway age.

They did not match perfectly. The models tended to start learning words a little late and then catch up faster, so the shape of the curve was only partly right.

The surprise in the paper is what happened when the researchers took replay away.

Coral’s household produced something like 10 million words a year, which is a rich environment by any measure. Hearing all of it once, in order, wasn’t enough. With a single pass the program barely learned words at all.

Around 25 to 30 passes over each day’s material was enough, and more than that added very little.

The researchers link this to what sleep is thought to do for memory. A program replaying audio files is not a sleeping infant, and the paper is careful about that.

The amount of recording mattered just as much. Fed only a tenth of Coral’s daily speech, under an hour a day, the program learned none of the checklist words by 24 months.

At 30% of the day, about two and a half hours, it learned 80 of the 649 checklist words.

At 70% it got about nine-tenths of the way to the full result. The rarer words, it seems, only turn up for a listener who is there most of the day.

One limitation shapes everything else. Household recordings are full of clattering dishes, television, and two people talking at once, and the program was not asked to cope with any of that.

Instead the researchers transcribed all the speech around each child, then had a text-to-speech system read the transcripts back as clean audio.

Each household got a mix of eight adult female voices, with 30% of segments read in a voice matched to the child’s mother.

So the word order, the timing and the vocabulary are real, and the sound isn’t. The acoustic problem a baby actually solves, picking one voice out of a noisy room, was left for later work.

Three of the eight children also had shorter recordings, 14 to 20 months of usable input, so their later trajectories are extrapolated rather than modeled.

The program also sees nothing: no faces, no pointing, no object being handed over, which is a large part of how toddlers work out what a word refers to.

The program learned sounds and words. It did not learn grammar, and whether the same machinery would arrive at sentence structure is the open question the authors name.

The team wants to use the setup for questions nobody can put to a real baby. What would less sleep do, or screen speech instead of a parent’s?

Future studies could also add eye contact and the rest of the social world the cameras captured but the model never saw.

Hadas Raviv, a computational cognitive scientist in Princeton’s psychology department who built the analysis pipeline, framed the goal as the opposite of the usual one in artificial intelligence.

“Unlike much of modern AI, which aims for superhuman performance, we’re trying to understand how humans learn and how that learning gives rise to intelligence,” Raviv said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease.

The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes.

Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" cells would.

To flip that switch in the cells, a molecule latches onto the spool that DNA is wound around, specifically near genes involved in sparking inflammation. That subtle molecular tweak "holds those genes poised for rapid activation," said Musa Mhlanga, a cell biologist and molecular geneticist at the Radboud Institute for Molecular Life Sciences in the Netherlands who wasn't involved in the new study.

However, scientists didn't know how that change was maintained over time.

The immune memory should have been destroyed soon after it was made, given that "the cell has enzymes whose entire job is to strip that mark off," Mhlanga told Live Science in an email. But somehow, the memory stuck. "So the obvious question was never really answered: how does a mark survive weeks or months against machinery actively removing it?" Mhlanga said.

The research focused on cells of the innate immune system, including macrophages (pictured), which gobble up germs, dead cells and cellular debris.

The new study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Science Immunology, may answer that question.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The research investigated the phenomenon in mouse immune cells and live lab mice, as well as some human cells in lab dishes. Past studies hinted that, when immune cells switch into their "primed" state, their metabolism changes. This, in turn, drives up the production of a molecule called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which has long been known to help regulate how DNA gets packaged in cells.

In this case, though, the molecule took on a surprising role, Mhlanga said. NAD+ usually gets used up when enzymes orchestrate chemical reactions. But when it comes to the enzymes that normally erase immune cells' memory, called KDM5a, that wasn't the case.

NAD+ latches onto that epigenetic eraser but doesn't get used up in the process; instead, it shuts down KDM5a, as if it were pushing an "off" button. By restraining its memory eraser, the immune cell remains in a primed and activated state, ready to ignite inflammation when triggered.

In experiments with mice, the researchers found that reducing or eliminating NAD+ from immune cells prevented them from entering this primed state. In mice with cancer, this hobbled the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells.

Additionally, in aging mice, the team observed that NAD+ levels dwindle in concert with the innate immune system's ability to respond to threats. The research builds a convincing "molecular bridge" between those two facts, Mhlanga said, raising a hypothesis for why immunity gets worse with age.

Broadly, the research adds to scientists' understanding of how innate immune cells enter this primed, inflammatory state. This line of research may help scientists understand "why some vaccines protect against diseases they were never designed for," Mhlanga said.

For example, a tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BDG) is thought to mount a broad immune response that may help stave off many conditions, from viral infections to Alzheimer's disease. (Some scientists think that Alzheimer's stems from a dysregulated immune response that BCG may help to normalize.)

While this line of research could have wide-ranging applications, the new study has some limitations. The researchers did a few experiments with human cells and backed up some of their findings in mice with data from human cancer patients. However, "the human data are thin by comparison with the mouse work," Mhlanga noted, so they bear further confirmation.

In the future, he'd be interested in studies exploring NAD+ in the context of the aging immune system, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The recent research hints that pushing NAD+ to optimal levels could help counter each of these conditions.

But especially in cancer, where the disease's biology varies by the tumour type and stage, "it is not a simple 'more NAD+ is better' story," he cautioned, "and I'd resist it being written as one."

#6457. Common fiber supplement eased knee arthritis pain and improved grip strength in six weeks

A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.

Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo. On a scale from zero to ten, their scores fell 1.11 points more.

Volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect. Those who followed a digital exercise program, or combined both treatments, did not.

The work was led by the University of Nottingham in England, and its results appeared in February 2026.

In 2019, about 528 million people worldwide were living with osteoarthritis, according to the World Health Organization. The knee is the joint most often affected, with 365 million cases.

About 33 million U.S. adults have the condition, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates. Physical exercise may help relieve pain and improve function, the agency notes.

In the U.K., 5.4 million people have knee osteoarthritis, according to a 2025 report from the charity Arthritis UK.

“Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis,” said Professor Lucy Donaldson, the charity’s director of research.

Under its former name, Versus Arthritis, the charity was one of the trial’s funders.

Between May 2022 and February 2025, the researchers randomly assigned 136 adults to four groups, and 117 completed all assessments.

Those who finished averaged 67.5 years of age, and 58.1 percent were women.

One group took 0.7 ounces (20 grams) of inulin powder a day. A second followed Joint Academy, a digital physical therapy program that began with a call to a personal physical therapist.

A third group combined both, and a fourth took maltodextrin, a starch-based powder, as a placebo. For ethical reasons linked to blood sugar, the placebo dose was half the inulin dose.

Volunteers did not know whether they were taking inulin or the placebo, but those assigned to exercise knew it. The staff who measured outcomes were blinded to all treatments.

Inulin’s pain result only just reached statistical significance, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.04 to 2.18 points.

Exercise lowered pain scores by 1.55 points compared with placebo, and the combination by 1.67 points. No added benefit from combining the two emerged, though the sample was too small to reliably detect one.

On average, both single treatments exceeded the one-point drop that patients typically notice as meaningful. Exercise came close to the two-point threshold for feeling “much better.”

A third of placebo takers also improved by at least one point, but only 11 percent improved by two points or more.

Inulin made people less sensitive to pressure and to repeated painful stimuli, two measures linked to how the nervous system processes pain. Exercise alone had no such effect.

“This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change – adding a fibre supplement to your breakfast or yogurt – could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function,” said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki of the University of Nottingham’s School of Medicine, the lead author.

Exercise improved a timed up-and-go test and a 30-second chair-stand test. Inulin alone had no effect on either.

Inulin feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. Only inulin raised blood levels of butyrate, one of those fatty acids, and of GLP-1, a hormone made in the gut.

Within the inulin groups, higher GLP-1 was associated with better grip strength, in an exploratory analysis that needs independent replication. The authors offer no explanation for the combined group’s grip result.

“The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation,” said Professor Ana Valdes, the senior author, also of the School of Medicine.

A 2024 Canadian trial of a similar fiber in adults with knee osteoarthritis and obesity reported gains in grip strength and mobility after six months. Its effect on knee pain was only a trend.

The short duration may not capture the full effects of exercise, the researchers acknowledged. Expectation effects in the exercise groups cannot be ruled out either.

Dropout reached 21 percent in the two exercise groups, compared with 3.6 percent in the two groups without exercise. To compensate, allocation odds were shifted toward exercise during later recruitment, which may have introduced bias.

A second analysis that included dropouts, with missing scores statistically imputed, gave consistent results. Only the effect of exercise on the up-and-go test lost statistical significance.

Of 50 inulin takers who finished, 23 reported minor digestive effects such as wind and bloating. None stopped the supplement or dropped out because of them.

U.K. government guidelines cited by the National Health Service call for 1.1 ounces (30 grams) of fiber a day, so the inulin dose alone supplied two-thirds of that.

Valdes sits on the scientific advisory boards of the nutrition company Chuckling Goat and of OLIPOP, roles declared unrelated to this study.

The study was published in the journal Nutrients.

#6456. The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.

About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.

It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.

The researchers argue that the regrowth marked the earliest stage of a new glaciation in North America, and that human-caused warming cut it short.

At the peak of the last glacial period, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Canada and reached into the northern United States.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” said Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory who led the study.

What’s left of it is the Barnes Ice Cap, on the central plateau of Baffin Island in Nunavut. Its bedrock is low for the Canadian Arctic, only about 1,640 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The ice has lasted this long because it is roughly 2,300 feet (700 meters) thick, enough to lift its surface to where snow survives the summer.

Young’s team wanted to know whether the ice cap had ever been smaller than it is today and then grown back. Gifford Miller of the University of Colorado Boulder was among the co-authors.

The answer matters beyond one ice cap, because models say glaciations over North America most likely begin on Baffin Island.

The Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the rock beneath it, so it doesn’t slide the way most glaciers do. Instead of grinding the ground as it spreads, it buries whatever is growing there and preserves it.

When the margin retreats, the moss and small plants it killed centuries ago come out of the ice.

Radiocarbon dating estimates when the plants died, giving researchers a way to date the ice’s advance.

Young’s team collected 88 of those plants at or near the 2022 ice edge. About 70% of them died around the year 1800, give or take 200 years. Those were the coldest summers of the Little Ice Age.

Sixteen more came from a half-mile (800-meter) line running out from the ice edge. A drained lake there had let the margin retreat farther than anywhere else.

In an interview with Earth.com, Young said that result surprised the team.

The researchers hadn’t expected the ice cap to have been smaller than it is now at any point in the last several thousand years.

“This unique finding allowed us to unexpectedly use these plants to track the ice cap’s renewed expansion,” Young noted.

The researchers also dated 35 boulders and bedrock surfaces around the ice cap. Rock that is open to the sky builds up a rare form of beryllium at a known rate.

The amount in a surface tells how long it has been uncovered.

All of the surfaces gave the same answer: the old ice sheet had retreated inside its 2022 position about 3,600 years ago.

The oldest plants along the half-mile line died around the year 1000, so the ice was already advancing by then.

To fill the gap, the team turned to 186 radiocarbon dates from plants under smaller ice caps on the same plateau. Not one of those dates is older than the Common Era.

The authors read that as the moment, roughly 2,000 years ago, when the summer snowline dropped onto the plateau and ice began to build up across it.

So the Laurentide reached its smallest size between about 3,000 and 2,000 years ago and then started to grow. The authors count that reversal as the start of the next glaciation.

The ice advanced in pulses during cold spells and was nearing its largest modern extent by about 1800.

By 1960 the growth had stopped. Aerial photographs show the margin retreating from about 1961, and the ice cap has since given up between 650 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) of ground.

Snow also survives the summer on less and less of it.

Around 1960, about 35% of its surface was high enough for snow to last through the summer. By the early 2000s only 3% was, and since 2010 none of it has been.

There is no longer any part of the ice cap where snow can pile up and turn into ice.

Summer temperatures have been climbing since the late 1700s, and since the early 1960s warmer summers account for almost all of the ice cap’s losses. Those summers track the greenhouse gases people have added to the air.

Between 1750 and 1850, the total rose by only about 12 parts per million of carbon dioxide equivalent. By 1960 it had risen another 50, and by 2024 another 138.

“The expansion and retreat of ice sheets has been one of Earth’s most consistent patterns over the last 2.6 million years,” Young told Earth.com.

About 2,000 years ago, he said, the Laurentide was starting its next phase of expansion, as it should have. Then greenhouse gases ended that expansion in the middle of the 20th century.

In the 1970s, some climate scientists argued that a new ice age was coming, and the idea got a famous airing in Newsweek.

Young said those scientists were essentially correct, even if the media twisted the story. “We did just barely start the next glaciation, but they didn’t know it at the time,” he said.

Behind that growth was a slow decline in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes, the orbital rhythm that paces ice ages.

Greenhouse gases did rise over those thousands of years, by about 20 parts per million. The authors found that was too small to overcome the cooling.

Computer models suggest the next glaciation will not begin for thousands of years. But those models usually define its start as the point where new ice sheets hold enough ice to lower the sea by about 10 feet (3 meters) or more.

Young’s team said that would miss the earlier stage of ice growth that his team considers the start of a glaciation.

A 2025 study built from ocean sediments and Earth’s orbit estimated that the first regrowth of ice in this interglacial would come somewhere in the last 1,800 years or so. The plants on Baffin Island agree.

What the record can’t yet say is exactly when the regrowth began. The plants that would date it are still under the ice, and only continued retreat will bring them out.

The dates so far are archived at the NSF Arctic Data Center.

Young said models of the ice cap’s future have it disappearing completely within the next few hundred years.

Asked what happens once the last piece of the Laurentide is gone, Young said another glaciation is unlikely anytime soon.

“Given the amount of greenhouse gases that are in the atmosphere and that we continue to pump, the next glaciation is a long way off,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6455. Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

In spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

After giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo says. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were big enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens said 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

It was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

The San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo says it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

The snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo says.

Since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added new ponds for breeding habitat.

Garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile says.

After the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans showed that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

The zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen said in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she said.

Head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are big enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

Each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

The rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

Disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She said a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”

The partners will not name the release sites. The zoo said secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she said.

Removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated new populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model said.

Raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she said.

The November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

There is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

The 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction plan.

More than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

Rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she said.

The mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

#6454. The 8 Best Pet Hair Vacuums Designed for Homes That Never Stop Shedding

We evaluated models from top brands including Dyson, Bissell, and Shark.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Getting pet hair out of carpets and off of tile and hardwood is a constant battle many are familiar with, and trying to remove those persistent hairs that have embedded themselves into your upholstery is another beast. Choosing the right vacuum can significantly improve your cleaning routine if you’re a cat or canine parent.

The top pet hair vacuums are designed with powerful suction and superior filtration (plus, they come with special attachments) to capture fine hair, thick fur, and pet dander. Regardless of whether you have a fluffy cat, a long-haired pup, or both, investing in a vacuum specifically made for pets will help you keep messes in check for a tidier home.

Upright and canister vacuums are the strongest options for deep cleaning, but cordless stick vacuums, handheld vacuums, and robot vacuums all aid in daily pet hair control. Units that have tangle-free brush rolls and easy-to-empty dustbins are best for reduced maintenance, and a HEPA filter is essential for clearing out dust and dander that may trigger your allergies.

I researched and hands-on-tested lots of vacuums to find versions that truly pick up pet hair, focusing on features, bin capacity, and filtration. Below are my choices, as well as advice and important pointers to consider before you shop.

I initially considered a range of vacuum styles, from uprights to robots to canisters. Keeping in mind different price points, I chose models that provide an optimal combination of suction strength, versatility, pet-focused features and tools, and value.

I tested the Shark AZ2002 Vertex in a home with two American Shorthair cats, three different floor types, and multiple area rugs. I cleaned everything from tracked litter and dust on laminate and carpet to pet hair on furniture and upholstery, trying out the different suction power modes and attachments as I went. I vetted the features that I thought would be most helpful for animal owners such as HEPA filtration, a motorized pet tool, and an anti-tangle brush roll. Based on this research and testing, these are my top recommendations for the best pet hair vacuums.

One of the things I liked most about this upright model is its specially crafted vacuum head, which uses both a soft roller brush and paddled, fin-like brush roll to pick up embedded hair, fine dust, and dirt from all types of flooring. I noticed that this method prevents longer hair from getting tangled in the brush roll and allows for a deeper clean overall.

Cleaning modes are easy to access with a simple switch on the handle, and the vacuum head has LED lights that illuminate hidden dust bunnies and stray pet hair, which was extremely helpful when cleaning under furniture and in corners.

Another major plus is that this upright model also converts into a motorized, lift-away pod for cleaning other surfaces like couch cushions and stairs. The vacuum’s hose stretches up to an impressive 12 feet, and it comes with a crevice tool and pet upholstery tool. I tried the motorized pet tool on polyester couch cushions, and it didn’t struggle to pick up embedded pet hair.

The Vertex has a large, 1-quart dustbin to accommodate more hair, along with a fully sealed HEPA filtration system to capture pet dander. And while it’s heavy, it navigates pretty easily.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Upright Vacuum Review

It’s hard to come by a vacuum that is less than $200 that doesn’t skimp on suction power, assets, or reliability. This model offers all of the above at an accessible price. Our tester has been using this vacuum for four years and has yet to be disappointed.

“This vacuum has a brush roll with multiple rows of bristles that kick out any hair that’s really deep inside a variety of fibers, including rugs and carpets.”

It works just as well on hardwood floors, and the swivel-steering vacuum head is easy to maneuver under and around furniture. The power cord is extremely long, extending 27 feet, and is automatically retractable with the cord rewind mechanism.

The CleanView comes with attachments for removing pet hair from stairs and hard-to-reach corners on hardwood and carpeted floors. It’s easy to empty, too, with a button on the front that releases dirt directly into the garbage.

One main complaint from our tester is that, given the size and weight of this upright model, it can be a pain to shuffle around as you clean. “Dragging around the Cleanview to different rooms of the house requires some effort. The vacuum weighs 15 pounds, which doesn’t seem like a lot until you need to get to a different part of your home.”

Full Bissell Cleanview Swivel Rewind Upright Vacuum Review

Dyson is most recognized for its powerful vacuums, and if you’re on the hunt for a machine that easily pulls pet hair out of your shaggiest of carpets, you won’t be disappointed with the Ball Animal 3 Extra model.

Besides strong suction, this vacuum boasts a five-layer, complete filtration system that captures dust and pet dander, preventing them from being released back into the air. The floor head has an integrated comb that untangles hair from the brush roll as it rotates, keeping lengthy strands from getting ensnared.

The vacuum is simple to handle thanks to the brand’s distinctive ball design, and it includes a combination tool, stair tool, turbine tool, and a pet groom tool. The wand is instant-release and has an extended hose for reaching isolated areas like underneath your couch or around dining room chairs.

This powerful vacuum has a sealed HEPA filtration system to securely trap dirt, dander, and fur so they don’t recirculate back into your home as you clean. It works on a variety of surfaces but handles hardwood floors the best because its good suction control prevents larger debris from scattering.

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser also has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors for months, I haven’t had to cut any hair from the bristles. Plenty of cat fur, dirt, and dander makes its way into the dustbin as the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I love that there is a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. It works well on couch cushions, and a few pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the vacuum converts into a canister pod, so it moves around easily as you work around your space.

The convertible design adds maneuverability, and the attachments included are helpful for more precise cleaning.

Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Full Review

The Bissell Pet Hair DualBrush packs two brush roll types into one vacuum. The first loosens and cleans debris that’s stuck to your floor or caught up in carpet fibers, and behind it, a second brush roll makes closer contact with the floor to pick up the now loosened debris. Powerful suction delivers strong pet hair pickup, too.

This model converts to a handheld-style canister vacuum that lifts off of the base, so you can easily clean hard-to-reach areas or furniture. We appreciate that this design also has LED lights on the vacuum floorhead and pet hair attachment to illuminate hidden dust and debris.

The DualBrush uses sensors to automatically detect the level of dirt and dust on the floor, and will adjust suction power accordingly, helping you get a deeper clean in situations where it’s most needed. It weighs 17 pounds, which may be a pain to push around for longer cleaning sessions, but that isn’t uncommon for an upright vacuum.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser DualBrush Upright Vacuum Review

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo comes with multiple features that are a standout for pet owners. This model is equipped with a HEPA filter to keep allergens out of your home, and the canister detaches from the base, making it easier to clean stairs, around baseboards, and along blinds. Just keep in mind that the hose only extends seven feet, so you’ll have to carry the detachable pod close by.

Some noteworthy attachments are a tangle-free brush roll and a motorized tool that’s specifically designed to remove pet hair from upholstery. The primary vacuum head has LED lights on the front and sides, and there’s also a crevice tool with an LED light for convenient cleaning in dark corners, along with a two-in-one dusting brush.

The vacuum has a touch-and-release button on the dustbin’s exterior to easily empty it without getting dust and pet dander on your hands.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo Lift-Off Upright Vacuum Review

Our tester has six pets, so there’s plenty of mess to go around, whether it’s tracked-in dirt from muddy paws or scattered litter. Pulling out the upright vacuum for quick cleanups isn’t always convenient, and this cordless stick model is her go-to for daily maintenance.

One of the things she loves the most about the Levoit LVAC-300 is the five-stage filtration system, which provides air purifier-level purification, a must-have for pet owners with animals that shed or have lots of dander.

The vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—so she was able to adjust suction power depending on the size of the mess and debris. The LVAC-300 transitions between floor types easily, but excels on hardwood and tile.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself.

Full LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Tired of the pet hair tumbleweeds strewn about your floors? This robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. With 16,200 pascals of suction power, it effectively picked up debris from a variety of floor types such as carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile.

One of the most notable features is the built-in razor in the base station that automatically slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have to manually remove hair from the brush roll.

Beyond that, our tester felt that this robot vacuum successfully avoided pet toys, cords, and overly friendly animals that seemed very interested in the vacuum’s whereabouts.

There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper mop, and they extend outward to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards.

The companion app is helpful for managing cleaning schedules, monitoring battery levels, and mapping, but gets a little more confusing as you adjust more advanced smart features.

Full Eureka J15 Pro Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

We’re regularly testing vacuums with focused pet hair features, so it’s common to see different vacuums take the place of others in this roundup. Here are a few that we’ve tested and think are still worth recommending:

Dyson V16 Piston Animal: This is a newer release from the brand, with some of the highest suction power we’ve seen from a cordless stick vacuum. The all-floor head cleaner excelled on carpet, and hair never got tangled around the brush roll, but performance on hard surfaces wasn’t as impressive. The vacuum comes with the classic Fluffy Optic soft roller cleaner head, but for the “all-floor” cleaner head isn’t the most ideal for all surfaces.

Miele Guard L1 Cat and Dog Bagged Canister Vacuum: The cleaner head on this vacuum lifts to five heights, and the extra-long hose allows you to work your way around your home without lugging the entire base vacuum around with you. On the downside, it doesn’t clean high-pile carpeting like shag or tufted wool, and other models we recommend have better pet-hair-specific attachments for cleaning upholstery.

There are a few factors that make a vacuum well-suited for dog and cat fur—namely, how much hair its bin holds, how it empties, how well it filters fine particles, and the types of attachments included.

The ideal bin capacity depends on the size of your home’s dimensions and the amount of pet hair you usually manage on a regular basis. For households with multiple pets, or animals that shed heavily, a vacuum with a spacious bin capacity (one liter or more) reduces the number of times you have to empty it during cleaning.

If you have a smaller home or you just have one pet, a bin capacity of 0.5 to 1 liter will most likely suffice. If you’re still unsure of what you might need, here’s a breakdown of the bin capacity each type of vacuum typically offers.

These normally have the largest capacity, ranging from two to four liters to hold more pet hair, dander, and debris before needing to be emptied. This design and capability could be ideal for heavy-duty cleaning or households with more than one pet.

Upright vacuums come in a close second, often with a capacity between one and three liters, so they’re a good option for folks with a pet that sheds mildly, or only during part of the year. These vacuums are also sufficient for standard home cleaning.

Because cordless vacuums are better used as supplementary cleaning tools, they have much smaller dustbins—usually ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 liters—which is really only enough for spot-cleaning, picking up dust bunnies between deep cleaning sessions, and use in tight spaces.

Similar to cordless vacuums, robot vacuums live on the smaller end of bin capacity. If you decide to go with this type, I recommend a model with a self-emptying bin. Most robot vacuums have small onboard dustbins, but they fill up faster. Self-emptying models have a larger dust collection area in the base, so you won’t have to manually empty as frequently.

For allergy sufferers, it’s essential to have a vacuum with an excellent filtration system, so look for models with a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter. These filters trap 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. Pet dander can be as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, and a HEPA filter efficiently captures these particles along with pollen, dust, and other allergens your pets may have tracked into the house.

A fully sealed filtration system, sometimes called an anti-allergen seal, is another common feature on pet vacuums. This means the components of the vacuum are tightly sealed so fine particles can’t escape back into your home once they’ve been sucked up.

Powerful suction is vital, but the included tools and attachments are often what pet owners use to successfully pull hair out of upholstery and carpeting. The following attachments are useful for tackling pet hair, and they come with many of the models I recommend above.

A standard attachment that comes with almost all vacuums, these elongated, narrow tools are great for accessing tight areas, like behind the toilet or between couch cushions. They’re useful for cleaning up clumps of hair that may have gathered in corners of your home where the vacuum’s floor head cannot reach.

Non-motorized upholstery brushes have bristles or a strip of microfiber to clean off furniture. As you pull the tool across fabric, the bristles lift pet hair and dust to be sucked up through the vacuum hose.

For pet hair that’s worked deep into upholstery, whether on your furniture or in your car, a motorized pet tool provides the most lifting power. These tools have small, spinning brush rolls, usually equipped with bristles, that agitate hair to pull it from the fabric, and they tend to work much more efficiently than non-motorized tools.

If you have pet hair or dander on your window screens or baseboards, a dusting brush has long, soft bristles that pick up dust and fine particles without scratching surfaces.

In addition to an arsenal of attachments to pull up pet hair, there are a few features that make cleaning up after your dog or cat even easier.

#6453. Grand Canyon hotels reopen 81 days after a deadly flood, echoing a 1966 disaster

Grand Canyon's South Rim hotels reopen November 20 after an August flash flood cut off their water. In 1966, a flood wrecked 40% of the same pipeline project.

For the first time since the end of August, visitors can book a hotel room on the South Rim of the Grand Canyon again.

On Friday, November 20, the South Rim’s hotels reopened to overnight guests, including El Tovar, which has stood on the edge of the canyon since 1905.

They had been closed for 81 days. A flash flood on August 29 tore through Bright Angel Canyon, killed two hikers and badly damaged the pipeline that carries water to the South Rim.

It was not the first time. In 1966, while that same pipeline was being built, a flood destroyed or carried off about 40% of the project, according to the National Park Service.

The park announced on November 18 that six South Rim lodges would reopen on November 20: El Tovar Hotel, Thunderbird Lodge, Kachina Lodge, Bright Angel Lodge and Maswik Lodge, along with Yavapai Lodge, which is operated by Delaware North.

On the same day, the park moved from Stage 4 to Stage 3 water conservation measures, which it called an important milestone in the restoration of South Rim water services.

Food and drink services will resume gradually, and the park is asking visitors to check its website for dining hours.

Conserving water is still important. Guests, visitors and residents are asked to take shorter showers, turn off faucets when they are not in use and avoid unnecessary water use.

The flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at about 2:30 p.m. on August 29. By the next morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Nearly all of the footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed.

Metal structures and debris washed into the Colorado River, which was closed to river traffic. In steep terrain, heavy rain can trigger flash floods in mountain rivers faster than expected.

Two hikers from Granbury, Texas, John Giusti, 46, and Brent Rosenkranz, 42, died in the flood.

A member of their hiking group was reported missing, and the park said in its September 8 update that one person remained unaccounted for.

The flood badly damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a 12½-mile pipeline built in the 1960s.

It carries water from Roaring Springs, on the North Rim side, down through the canyon and up to the South Rim, where it supplies drinking water and fire protection for every facility, including more than 800 historic buildings.

The park’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to more than 6 miles of caves.

About 40% of the old pipeline between the Phantom Ranch area and the North Rim was damaged, and the water intakes at Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs were hit hard.

On August 31, the park stopped all overnight stays at its hotels, including Phantom Ranch, and the South Rim began living on stored water.

The park stayed open for day visits. When it announced the closure, it said South Rim food and drink services, the Grand Canyon Clinic and the post office would remain open, some with reduced hours, while campers could only dry camp.

On September 16, a second flash flood damaged a temporary water intake that crews were building at Bright Angel Creek.

No one was hurt, but crews had to work out what repairs were needed and how the damage would affect the timeline.

On September 19, the park said it expected to start pumping water from the creek to a new treatment plant by November 16, and it was working on an agreement to haul about 200,000 gallons of water a day to keep its tanks from running low.

At the time, the South Rim was using about 137,000 gallons a day.

By November 18, the park said water services to the South Rim were being restored, which allowed the hotels to reopen two days later.

The pipeline itself was born out of a water problem. From 1901 to 1932, the Santa Fe railroad brought drinking water to the South Rim by train every day, and the trains came back as needed until the late 1960s.

In the summer of 1961, a water train of 20 cars carried about 204,000 gallons.

Construction of the Transcanyon Waterline began in January 1965, using 6-inch and 8-inch aluminum pipe. Most of the equipment was designed specifically for the project, and the rest of the work was done by hand.

A year later, the project was nearly finished when what the park calls a 1,000-year flood struck.

Fifteen inches of rain fell on the inner canyon, and the water carried away trees, boulders and sections of new pipe.

A survey after the flood found that about 40% of the project was destroyed or missing. The cost rose from $2 million to $5 million, and construction resumed in late 1967.

The flood’s high-water mark is still recorded on the walls of the Phantom Ranch Ranger Station.

The old line was built to last about 30 years and has been in service for more than 50. Since 2010, it has suffered over 85 major breaks.

A single repair often costs more than $25,000, and crews can reach the inner canyon only by trail or helicopter.

Breaks had closed the hotels before. In December 2025, after three significant breaks since late October, the park suspended overnight stays on December 6 and reopened the lodges on December 17.

In 2023, the park began a $208 million project to replace the pipeline and modernize the water system.

The new pipeline on the south side of the canyon was not damaged by either flood this year, and before August 29 the park was just over a month away from starting to use it.

Some inner canyon trails reopened in late October, including the South Kaibab Trail below the Tipoff and the River Trail.

But the Black Bridge, the Silver Bridge, Phantom Ranch and the entire North Kaibab Trail remained closed, and the park warned that water would stay off at Mile-and-a-Half and Three-Mile Resthouses and at Havasupai Gardens for the rest of the winter.

Hikers must carry all their water and a way to filter or treat it.

El Tovar, a National Historic Landmark since 1987, was built from local limestone and Oregon pine for nearly $250,000. The hotel, which has 78 rooms, is once again taking guests.

The park says water conservation remains important as operations resume, and that the patience of residents, visitors and businesses during the emergency helped it keep essential services running.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s releases on the reopening of South Rim lodging, the August 29 flash flood, the recovery plan, the projected water dates, the August 31 hotel closure, the two hikers who died, the second flash flood, the trail reopenings and the December 2025 hotel reopening, its pages on the Transcanyon Waterline and its history, and its page on El Tovar Hotel.

#6452. A brain region known for listening helps us speak

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Recordings reveal how Wernicke’s area helps turn thoughts into words

A small bit of brain has big roles in understanding and producing speech, a new study finds.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.
